title: Write-Aware Timestamp Tracking: Effective and Efficient Page Replacement for Modern Hardware
one_line: WATT is a buffer-pool page-replacement policy that keeps a bounded per-page log of read and write timestamps, scores pages by the maximum of their sub-frequencies plus a tunable write penalty, and picks victims by lock-free random sampling with AVX2-accelerated value computation.

repo.evidence: Paper p.1: 'PVLDB Artifact Availability: ... https://github.com/leanstore/leanstore/tree/WATT'. The WATT branch exists (GitHub API /repos/leanstore/leanstore/branches -> WATT @ 8140750f8ca6487c4165d5ecf6cfb28d3873d2aa), its head commit (2023-09-27, 'add VLDB presentation, transcript and video') is authored by Demian Voehringer <demian.voehringer@fau.de>, the paper's first author, and it contains the real implementation (backend/leanstore/storage/buffer-manager/BufferFrame.hpp: struct alignas(64) Tracker with reads[kr=8]/writes[kw=4], SIMD getValue(); PageProviderThread.cpp: findThreshold() + globalTrackerTime++). Its README links itodnerd/WATT-Overview, which links the official simulator (itodnerd/WATT-simulate) and traces (itodnerd/WATT-traces). CAVEAT: the clone in repo/ is the default branch 'master' (repo/.git/packed-refs has only refs/remotes/origin/master @ 90fcf185) and contains NO WATT code -- grep for 'WATT' over repo/ returns no matches. Use 'git clone -b WATT'.
repo.badge_evidence: Paper p.1 'PVLDB Artifact Availability' statement pointing at https://github.com/leanstore/leanstore/tree/WATT; no PVLDB reproducibility / ACM 'Results Reproduced' badge found for PVLDB vol. 16 issue 11.

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official, MIT-licensed, and contains the actual system on the WATT branch: BufferFrame.hpp holds struct Tracker (atomic reads[8]/writes[4], readPos/writePos, trackRead/trackWrite/merge/getValue, simd_getFreq with _mm256_min_ps, table_8/table_4 = Listing 3's iQuotient) and PageProviderThread.cpp holds findThreshold(int samples), a __builtin_prefetch batch loop, and BufferFrame::globalTrackerTime++ (= Listing 2). Simulator (itodnerd/WATT-simulate: algos/{WATT.cpp,ARC.hpp,hyperbolic.hpp,lean_evict.hpp,cf_lru.hpp,lru_wsr.hpp,lru_k.hpp,CLOCK.hpp,lru.hpp,random.hpp} + evalAccessTable/evalAccessTable.cpp) and traces (itodnerd/WATT-traces) are separate official repos linked from that README. Not a placeholder, not binary-only. Caveat: repo/ is the master branch and has zero WATT code (grep for 'WATT' in repo/ = no matches; repo/README.md lists io/blob/latency/mvcc/btw/cidr branches but not WATT).

H2_no_root.evidence: Entirely user-space C++: buffer pool is anonymous mmap (repo/backend/leanstore/storage/buffer-manager/BufferManager.cpp:41) with only advisory madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE|MADV_DONTFORK) (:48-50); I/O is O_RDWR|O_DIRECT on a plain file (repo/backend/leanstore/LeanStore.cpp:60) plus libaio in AsyncWriteBuffer.cpp. No kernel module, eBPF, KVM, RDMA, /proc/sys write or hugepage reservation anywhere. repo_facts.json red flags resolve benignly: the 'sudo' hits are apt-get lines in repo/README.md:9 and .github/workflows/ccpp.yml:17 (libaio/tbb are buildable/conda-installable in $HOME), and the single 'perf_counters' hit (repo/shared-headers/PerfEvent.hpp:100 perf_event_open) FAILS SOFT -- PerfEvent.hpp:101-106 prints 'Error opening counter' and does events.resize(0); names.resize(0); return; -- and is switchable off via DEFINE_bool(cpu_counters, true) at repo/backend/leanstore/Config.cpp:25. The only privileged call, setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS,0,-20) at BufferManager.cpp:91, is gated by DEFINE_bool(root, false) (Config.cpp:29). Cost of perf_event_paranoid=3: Figure 11 (cycles/instructions/L1/branch misses per TX) is not reproducible.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: CPU-only, no GPU, single node. The Section 4 simulation runs at FULL paper scale on one core (Table 2: 1-2 M accesses over 10k-66k pages; WATT-traces TPC_C/trace.csv = 11.2 MB). Section 6 needs scale-down: the paper used an EPYC 7713 (64c/128t), 512 GB RAM and a 3.8 TB PM1733 with 400 GB YCSB and 264/588 GB TPC-C (Sec. 6.1), vs 16c/32t, 125 GB RAM and ~257 GB free here. The mechanism is a ratio effect -- Figure 1 sweeps buffer-pool/dataset from 1% to 100% -- so a 2 GB pool over a 100 GB YCSB dataset reproduces the paper's exact 8GB/400GB = 2% regime with 24 workers and 1-8 evictors, and TPC-C at ~400 warehouses (~66 GB) replaces 1600 wh. Not reproducible at any scale: TPC-C 3200 wh (588 GB > free disk) and Figure 12's 32-evictor-thread point (16 physical cores).

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: Dependencies are user-space installable: gflags/tabulate/rapidjson are auto-fetched at configure time by CMake ExternalProject_Add from github.com (repo/libs/gflags.cmake:9-21), and repo/backend/CMakeLists.txt:25 links only 'gflags Threads::Threads aio tbb atomic tabluate rapidjson' -- TBB is on conda-forge and libaio builds into $HOME with 'make prefix=$HOME/local install'. gcc 12.2 / cmake 3.25 on the machine satisfy C++20 + -mavx2 (repo/CMakeLists.txt:13,18); AVX-512 is opt-in only (Config.cpp:62 btree_hints). Data: all five Section 4 traces are public at github.com/itodnerd/WATT-traces (WATT_competition_traces/{TPC_C,TPC_E,ZipfRO,dynZipfRO,dynZipfRW}/trace.csv, Git-LFS, format 'pages,is_write'), and the YCSB/TPC-C datasets of Section 6 are generated in-process by frontend/ycsb/ycsb.cpp and frontend/tpc-c/tpcc.cpp. No proprietary trace, no model weights, no gated download. Minor friction: git-lfs must be unpacked into $HOME; frontend/CMakeLists.txt still defines a rocksdb_tpcc target (RocksDB, liburing, snappy, zstd) so build 'make -j ycsb tpcc' rather than 'make -j'.

reproduce.target: Figure 1 (p. 5) plus Figure 2 (p. 6) -- the Section 4 simulation claim that WATT has the lowest miss count on average across 9 competitors x 5 traces x buffer-pool ratios (Goal 1), and that raising write_weight cuts writes by >10% on TPC-C (20% on TPC-E) for <15% (7%) more misses (Goal 2). Secondary: Figure 9 (p. 10), reads/writes per TX in LeanStore (LeanEvict +12% reads / +26% writes, Hyperbolic +5% / +11%, Random +11% / +36% vs WATT).
reproduce.scale_down: None needed for Figure 1/2: the five traces are 1-2 M accesses over 10k-66k pages and the sweep is embarrassingly parallel over 32 threads. For the secondary Figure 9: YCSB with target_gib=100 and dram_gib=2 (preserves the paper's 8GB/400GB = 2% buffer-pool ratio), worker_threads=24, pp_threads=4, run_for_seconds=1200 x 2 reps; TPC-C at ~400 warehouses (~66 GB) instead of 1600/3200 wh; --cpu_counters=false. Figure 11 (hardware counters) and the 32-evictor point of Figure 12 are dropped.
reproduce.effort: Figure 1 + Figure 2: ~3 person-days + ~20-40 CPU-hours. Adding the scaled-down Figure 9: +5-7 person-days + ~15 machine-hours of benchmark runs plus ~4 h of dataset generation.
reproduce.rationale: The simulator is a self-contained CMake C++ program whose configurations for Figures 1-8 are hard-coded in evalAccessTable/evalAccessTable.cpp (sweeps for randSize 1-64, KR 1-64, epochs {1..128,max}, dampening 0-100 step 5, aggregation {min,avg,median,max,lucas}, KW, write cost 0-200 step 5), it emits a CSV of algorithm/ram_size/elements/reads/writes, the traces are public and tiny, the repo was last pushed 2025-06-30, and the whole thing fits at paper scale on this machine. Only friction: no plotting scripts shipped (re-plot in Python) and a git-lfs fetch. The LeanStore half on its own would be M -- the driver cloned the wrong branch, libaio/TBB must come from source/conda, a bare 'make -j' breaks on the rocksdb_tpcc target, no run scripts pin the Section 6.1 flag sets, the policy-selection mechanism on the WATT branch could not be settled by desk review, and a dataset/thread scale-down is mandatory.

addons.name: self-tuning-write-weight
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing WATT's fixed write_weight with a closed-loop controller driven by measured device read/write service times and the evictor's dirty-page backlog improves end-to-end TX/s (and lowers host write volume at equal throughput) under workloads whose write intensity changes over time (YCSB alternating 100R and 70R/30W phases, TPC-C with a growing dataset), compared with the paper's fixed write_costs = 4.
addons.mechanism: Add EWMA counters for per-page write-completion latency and pread latency plus evictor stall time in AsyncWriteBuffer. Once per epoch (at the existing globalTrackerTime++ site in the evictor) step write_costs multiplicatively in the direction that lowers estimated I/O service time per eviction, or, in 'endurance mode', drives measured host writes/s toward a configured budget. The data-plane change is one expression: Tracker::getValue() already returns readFreq + writeFreq * FLAGS_write_costs, so FLAGS_write_costs becomes a relaxed-atomic double. Pre-screen the control law in WATT-simulate, whose driver already sweeps write cost 0-200.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 4.3: 'Because write costs depend on the used hardware and workload, the page value function of WATT includes a write_weight parameter' -- yet the paper fixes it at 4 from Figure 8 and never varies it in Section 6. Figure 8 shows total I/O is non-monotonic in write_weight with a different optimum per workload (TPC-C / TPC-E / dynZipfRW). The artifact default is even different from the paper's (backend/leanstore/Config.cpp on the WATT branch: DEFINE_uint32(write_costs, 1, ...)), which itself suggests the constant is not settled.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Localized: one expression in Tracker::getValue(), a few dozen lines of controller at the existing epoch-advance site, and counters in AsyncWriteBuffer -- far under 1k LOC touching three files. Evaluable with the existing ycsb/tpcc frontends at the Section 4 scale-down described above, and cheaply pre-screened in the authors' own simulator. Clearly doable by 2-4 students in 10 weeks.
addons.research_value_rationale: It removes the paper's one admitted hardware- and workload-dependent knob and targets SSD endurance, which VLDB reviewers care about, and the closed-loop version is genuinely absent from the artifact. But cost-aware self-adaptive buffer replacement is an established family (CASA/ACR/FD-Buffer), so the contribution is the setting -- sampling-based, many-core, NVMe, measured rather than assumed R/W cost ratio -- rather than the idea itself.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'self-tuning adaptive write penalty cost-aware buffer replacement flash database online controller 2024 2025'; Semantic Scholar citation list of DOI 10.14778/3611479.3611529 (11 citing papers, none on adaptive write weighting). Closest prior art is the CASA / ACR (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/221422739_ACR_An_Adaptive_Cost-Aware_Buffer_Replacement_Algorithm_for_Flash_Storage_Devices) / FD-Buffer (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/264561687_FD-Buffer_A_Cost-Based_Adaptive_Buffer_Replacement_Algorithm_for_Flash_Memory_Devices) line from 2010-2015 -- single-threaded, LRU-list based, embedded-flash era, and not cited by WATT. Nothing applies an online cost controller to a sampling-based many-core NVMe buffer manager.

addons.name: epoch-clock-decoupling
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that advancing WATT's global epoch on min(evictions, buffer-pool accesses, wall-clock) rather than on eviction count alone reduces read misses after a workload phase change, under workloads that alternate between an in-memory phase (eviction stalls, so the clock freezes) and an out-of-memory phase, compared with the paper's eviction-driven epoch clock.
addons.mechanism: Today globalTrackerTime++ fires only inside the page-evictor loop after cacheSize/epoch_size evictions (Listing 2 step 3). When the working set temporarily fits in RAM the evictor sleeps, the clock stops, and every resident page's age t_now - t_i freezes, so on resumption a page last touched at the start of the quiet period scores identically to one touched at the end. Add a second clock source -- a padded shared access counter aggregated from per-worker counters, or a coarse CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE read on the evictor's wake path -- that can also advance the epoch, with the combined epoch rate capped so the cache-line ping-pong argument of Section 5.1 still holds. Measure the ping-pong cost directly, since contention is the stated reason epochs exist.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 3.2: 'An approach we found to work well is to couple the growth of t_now to the number of pages replaced.' Figure 5 sweeps only how many epochs per full RAM replacement, never the source of the clock, and Section 5.1 justifies epochs purely by contention avoidance. Neither the simulation (trace replay with no idle time) nor Section 6 (steady-state 20-minute runs at a fixed 8 GB pool, Sec. 6.1) ever exercises a stalled-eviction phase, so the assumption is untested. The WATT branch's DEFINE_uint32(epoch_size, 1000) is also far from the paper's tuned '4 epochs per full RAM replacement', another sign the clock design is unsettled.
addons.feasibility_rationale: A shared counter plus a few lines at the epoch-advance site and in the evictor's sleep/wake path; Tracker::trackRead already early-outs on 'now != reads[pos]' so the data plane is untouched. The phase-alternating workload is a small driver change in frontend/ycsb/ycsb.cpp, and the idea can be pre-screened in WATT-simulate by injecting idle gaps into the public traces. Uses the existing harness end to end.
addons.research_value_rationale: It attacks a core, undocumented design assumption of the algorithm and both outcomes are informative -- if the eviction-driven clock turns out to be robust to stalls, that explains something real about why WATT works. It is a gap in the paper's otherwise thorough parameter study rather than a headline contribution, so a reviewer would rate it solid rather than surprising.

scoop_check.details: Queries: Semantic Scholar citations of DOI 10.14778/3611479.3611529 (11 papers: ScaleEvict DaMoN'26, Predictive Translation SIGMOD'26, Hitchhike ASPLOS'26, How to Write to SSDs VLDB'26, Scalable Far Memory SOSP'25, Sampling-based Predictive Database Buffer Management VLDB'25, Lock-Free Throughput-Optimized Cache Eviction SIGMETRICS'25, LeanStore VLDB'24, DEX VLDB'24, Latency Hiding VLDB'23 -- none revisits the epoch clock); 'epoch clock page replacement buffer manager eviction rate coupled'. Nothing found.

addons.name: write-aware-quick-demotion-vs-watt
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a write-aware quick-demotion policy (S3-FIFO-style sharded small/main FIFO queues with a dirty-page penalty applied at demotion) matches or beats WATT's combined miss and write counts on the paper's five traces and on YCSB/TPC-C inside LeanStore, while using <=2 bytes of per-page metadata instead of WATT's 50, under out-of-memory OLTP workloads.
addons.mechanism: (i) In WATT-simulate, add an s3fifo policy next to the existing sieve.hpp, parameterised by a write_cost that re-inserts a dirty page once on demotion from the small queue -- a quick-demotion analogue of Eq. 3 -- and run it through the driver's existing sweep grid. (ii) In LeanStore, replace the evictor's sample-and-threshold step (findThreshold + the prefetch batch loop) with per-partition ring buffers of frame pointers; LeanStore already shards frames into 1<<partition_bits partitions, so the paper's Goal-4 claim that FIFO queues cannot scale can be tested rather than assumed. Shrink BufferFrame::Header::Tracker to a 2-bit frequency counter plus the existing dirty indicator. (iii) Report misses, writes, evictions/s, TX/s and metadata bytes per page side by side against WATT, Hyperbolic, LeanEvict and Random.
addons.motivating_evidence: WATT's competitor set (Table 1: random, CLOCK, LeanEvict, LRU2, LRU, CFLRU, LRU_WSR, Hyperbolic, ARC) is entirely pre-2018. S3-FIFO (SOSP'23) and SIEVE (NSDI'24) are concurrent work claiming ARC-beating effectiveness with ~1 bit of metadata and no list-head contention, which directly contests WATT's premise that 'storing more information should lead to more accurate page replacement' (Sec. 3). WATT carries the largest metadata cost in the paper's own table (50 B/page, 1.2% at 4 KB pages, Sec. 3.2) and is not the fastest evictor in Figure 10 (Hyperbolic is ahead). The authors themselves added algos/sieve.hpp to WATT-simulate after publication, so they treat the comparison as open. Figure 1 also contains red panels where competitors beat WATT.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The simulator half is a drop-in algos/ file evaluated by the existing sweeps. The LeanStore half is cross-cutting: it replaces the victim-selection path, changes the buffer-frame header layout, and needs a correctness shakeout under LeanStore's optimistic version locks, plus the full scaled-down Section 6 harness (which ships no run scripts) for the TX/s comparison. Realistic for 2-4 students in 10 weeks, but it is the bulk of the project rather than a side change.
addons.research_value_rationale: A VLDB reviewer would care on two counts: it tests whether WATT's rich per-page timestamp history actually earns its 50 B/page against a fair modern baseline the paper could not have included, and it produces what appears to be the first write-aware quick-demotion policy for a DBMS buffer pool. Both outcomes teach something -- 'WATT still wins, and here is why per-page history beats quick demotion on OLTP page traces' is as publishable as the converse, and either way the community gets the missing WATT-vs-S3-FIFO/SIEVE data point.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'write-aware S3-FIFO flash SSD buffer pool eviction dirty page penalty 2025'; 'SIEVE database buffer manager write aware'; Semantic Scholar citations of DOI 10.14778/3611479.3611529. Found ECR: eviction-cost-aware cache management for page-level flash SSDs (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpe.5395, 2021 -- chip-queue-latency aware, LRU family, not quick demotion) and S3-FIFO itself (https://s3fifo.com/blog/2023/08/01/fifo-queues-are-all-you-need-for-cache-eviction/ -- key-value caches, write-oblivious, no DBMS buffer pool). Also adjacent but different: Using Lock-Free Design for Throughput-Optimized Cache Eviction (SIGMETRICS'25, cites WATT, targets eviction-path concurrency not policy effectiveness). No work combines quick demotion with a write penalty in a DBMS buffer manager, and none benchmarks S3-FIFO/SIEVE against WATT.

addons.name: bounded-ghost-trackers
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that retaining a memory-bounded ghost history of the WATT tracker for recently evicted pages (<=2% of buffer-pool bytes) reduces read misses under small buffer-pool ratios (1-10% of dataset) and shifting-hot-set workloads (dynZipfRO, TPC-C), compared with WATT's stateless re-admission, and captures most of the benefit of the unbounded history that is already present but unevaluated in the artifact.
addons.mechanism: The WATT branch already contains struct Tracker_store (non-atomic, serialisable) and struct WATT_LOG { std::vector<Tracker_store> pid_trackers; store(PID, const Tracker&); load(PID, Tracker&); } with a static WATT_LOG watt_backlog, gated by DEFINE_bool(watt_history, false) and sized by DEFINE_uint32(watt_log_size, 0, 'what is the largest expected page_id') -- i.e. an O(dataset) array, which is presumably why no figure reports it. Replace it with a fixed-capacity sharded open-addressing table of (PID, Tracker_store) with CLOCK/FIFO eviction of ghost entries, sized as a fraction of the buffer pool; call load() on page-in (before BufferFrame::reset clears the tracker's successor) and store() on evict; age ghost timestamps against the current epoch so stale ghosts decay instead of resurrecting cold pages. Sweep ghost capacity 0 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 5 / unbounded percent and report misses, writes and memory, including the fair comparison where ghost bytes are charged against buffer-pool bytes.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 3.2 bounds the history of each resident page but the paper never discusses what happens on eviction: a page read back in starts with an empty log. In the Section 6.1 regime (8 GB pool over a 400 GB dataset, i.e. 2%) nearly every access is to a page with no history, which undercuts the paper's own thesis in Section 3 that 'storing more information should lead to more accurate page replacement'. ARC -- the one competitor that keeps ghost lists -- is the strongest rival in Figure 1 and wins in several panels. The artifact's unevaluated FLAGS_watt_history/WATT_LOG shows the authors considered this and stopped at an O(dataset) prototype.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Both the data structure and the two call sites exist in skeleton form on the WATT branch; the work is bounding memory, adding ghost-entry eviction and epoch-aging, and wiring load()/store() into the page-in and evict paths -- a few hundred LOC in three files. Pre-screenable in WATT-simulate, which already implements ghost-list policies in algos/ARC.hpp. Runs on the existing ycsb/tpcc frontends at the scale-down above.
addons.research_value_rationale: It closes a real gap between the paper's thesis and its implementation, and the outcome is not obvious: ghost entries consume bytes that could have held real 4 KB pages, so the classic ARC trade-off lands very differently at page granularity than in web caches, and the artifact's own author left it unfinished. But 'add ghost lists' is a well-trodden mechanism, so a reviewer would call the result solid rather than surprising.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'ghost list evicted page history sampling-based eviction hyperbolic caching improve reinsertion 2024 2025'; Semantic Scholar citations of DOI 10.14778/3611479.3611529. Ghost lists are standard (ARC FAST'03, 2Q VLDB'94) and there are patents on ghost-list adjustment factors, but nothing applies them to sampled, timestamp-log page values or evaluates a memory-bounded ghost tracker inside a DBMS buffer pool. The closest citing work, Sampling-based Predictive Database Buffer Management (PVLDB 18(13):5569-5581, 2025, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~r9guo/publication/pbm.html), is also sampling-based but predicts future accesses from long-running scans rather than retaining past history -- related, not the same.

risks: Wrong branch cloned: repo/ is leanstore 'master' and contains no WATT code at all (grep for 'WATT' returns nothing; repo/README.md does not list a WATT branch). Every code_location above exists by the same path on both trees, but on master the contents are the LeanEvict implementation. Anyone acting on this report must re-clone with 'git clone -b WATT'.

The artifact is frozen at 2023-09-27 and forked from the pointer-swizzling LeanStore, which upstream has since replaced with the vmcache design (PVLDB'24, repo/README.md:55). The WATT branch will get no upstream fixes, and porting WATT to modern LeanStore would be a project in itself.

perf_event_paranoid=3 makes Figure 11 (cycles / instructions / L1 misses / branch misses per TX) unreproducible. Goal 3 (CPU efficiency) can only be checked via evictions/s (Figure 10) and wall-clock TX/s (Figure 13). The code degrades gracefully (PerfEvent.hpp:101-106) so this blocks a figure, not the build.

16 physical cores vs the paper's 64: Figure 12 sweeps to 32 evictor threads and Figures 9/13 use 120 workers. Multi-core scalability (Goal 4) can only be tested to ~16 threads and any result must be presented as a 16-core restatement, not a reproduction.

~257 GB free disk rules out TPC-C 1600 wh (264 GB), TPC-C 3200 wh (588 GB) and YCSB 400 GB. Buffer/dataset ratios can be preserved but absolute-scale effects (SSD internal GC, queue depth at ~1M IOPS) cannot be reproduced.

Shared machine: 111 of 125 GiB RAM free at measurement time and the NVMe pair is shared. Out-of-memory storage-engine benchmarks are very sensitive to co-tenant I/O; runs must be repeated and interleaved, copying the paper's median-of-2400-samples methodology (Sec. 6.2).

No run or plot scripts ship with either repo. The Section 6.1 flag sets must be reconstructed from prose plus the README example command line, and desk review could not determine how the WATT branch selects between WATT / Hyperbolic / Random / LeanEvict (flag vs compile-time switch) -- budget a day for this.

Traces are Git-LFS pointers; git-lfs must be unpacked into $HOME and the repo's LFS bandwidth quota must hold. The Zipf traces could be regenerated from Sec. 4.1, but the TPC-C/TPC-E traces (instrumented Shore-MT) could not.

Same-group scoop pressure: the Leis group publishes continuously on LeanStore buffer management (LeanStore PVLDB'24; How to Write to SSDs PVLDB'26; Predictive Translation SIGMOD'26). A natural fifth add-on -- NVMe-aware out-of-place writeback to cut device write amplification, motivated by the paper measuring only host write volume and by the unevaluated FLAGS_out_of_place -- is already scooped by How to Write to SSDs (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol19/p1469-lee.pdf, artifact github.com/LeeBohyun/ZLeanStore) and would also need privileged nvme smart-log access to measure device WAF.

Unresolved implementation detail: the WATT branch's SIMD page-value path clamps subfrequencies with _mm256_min_ps(div, one), which does not appear in Eq. 1 or Listing 3. Its effect on the published numbers is unknown and must be checked before claiming a reproduction.
